hints: Focus on the definition of Km in the question: it is the substrate concentration needed to reach half of Vmax, so ask yourself what that tells you about how easily the enzyme binds substrate.
If an enzyme has low affinity, it binds substrate poorly, so think about whether you would need a little or a lot of substrate to get it working at half speed and then at full speed.
walkthrough:
**Remember what Km actually measures**

Think of Km as a helpful number, not just a letter. It is the substrate concentration $[S]$ that gives half the maximum rate.

Key rule:
$$K_m = [S] \text{ when } V = \frac{V_{max}}{2}$$

**Link affinity to Km**

High affinity means the enzyme grabs substrate very easily, so only a little substrate is needed to reach half speed. That is a low Km.

Low affinity is the opposite. The enzyme binds poorly, so you need a lot more substrate to reach half speed. That is a high $K_m$.

**Link affinity to reaching Vmax**

Vmax is when every active site is full. If affinity is low, it is hard to fill those sites.

So you must keep adding more and more substrate to finally saturate the enzyme. That means Vmax is only reached at a high substrate concentration.

options.A: Correct. Low affinity means poor binding, so high Km and a need for high substrate concentration to saturate the enzyme and reach Vmax.
options.B: High Km is right for low affinity, but Vmax at low substrate concentration is wrong because a poorly binding enzyme needs lots of substrate to become saturated.
options.C: Low Km is wrong here because low Km means high affinity, the enzyme would work well even with little substrate.
options.D: This describes the opposite enzyme, one with high affinity, which has low Km and reaches Vmax easily at low substrate concentration.
